title: Recording dental & periodontal charting
blurb: FDI and Palmer notation, tooth surfaces, charting symbols, pocket charts, and recording exactly what the dentist calls.
question: During a check-up the dentist calls: 'Three-six, MO caries. Four-six, root filled. One-eight missing.' Then, probing the gums, 'Bleeding, two-six distobuccal.' What exactly do you record, and where on the chart?

teach.body: A dental chart is a map of the patient's mouth: which teeth are present, missing, decayed, filled or crowned, and what treatment is planned. A periodontal chart maps the gums: pocket depths, bleeding, recession and mobility. The dentist examines and calls out findings; you record them accurately, at the correct tooth and surface. The chart becomes part of the legal clinical record, so it must be accurate, legible and made at the time.

teach.h: FDI notation: two digits, quadrant first
teach.body: The FDI system gives every tooth a two-digit number. The first digit is the quadrant; the second is the tooth, counting back from the midline (1 = central incisor, 8 = third molar). Permanent quadrants are 1 upper right, 2 upper left, 3 lower left, 4 lower right. Baby (deciduous) teeth use quadrants 5 to 8 and tooth numbers 1 to 5. Say each digit separately: 36 is 'three-six', not 'thirty-six'.

teach.caption: The chart is drawn as you face the patient, so the patient's RIGHT is on the LEFT of the chart. Highlighted: 36, the lower left first molar.

teach.h: Name the surface, then the tooth
teach.caption: Mesial faces the midline, distal faces away. Back teeth have an occlusal (biting) surface; front teeth an incisal edge. Upper teeth have a palatal surface, lower teeth a lingual one.

teach.caption: This lesson uses one common convention: red for treatment needed, blue or black for existing work. Symbols and colours do vary between practices and software, so in practice always follow your own system.

teach.body: Before periodontal charting, have a graduated periodontal probe ready. The dentist probes six points on each tooth: three on the buccal side (mesiobuccal, buccal, distobuccal) and three on the lingual or palatal side. At each point they call the pocket depth in millimetres, and any bleeding on probing. Bleeding on probing is the key sign of active gum inflammation. They also call recession, mobility and furcation involvement.

teach.caption: Each number is a pocket depth in mm; BOP marks bleeding called at that exact site. Colour shows depth: green up to 3 mm, orange 4 to 5 mm, red 6 mm or more. Charted as you face the patient, so for 26 the mesial side is on the left. Repeat charting at review shows whether the gums are responding.

rows.label: Grade I
values: Up to 1 mm side to side

teach.caption: Furcation is the area between the roots of a multi-rooted tooth. It shows up as * on a BPE.

teach.text: Record EXACTLY what the dentist calls, at the site they call it. Never 'correct' a call or chart what you think you see. If you missed a call or aren't sure, ask for it to be repeated. If YOU notice something suspicious, such as an ulcer or a lump, record it and tell the dentist.

items: FDI: quadrant then tooth. 1 UR, 2 UL, 3 LL, 4 LR; deciduous 5 to 8 with teeth 1 to 5.
The chart faces you: the patient's right is on the chart's left.
Surfaces: M, D, O or I, B or La, L or P. Code cavities by surface, e.g. MO.
Pocket charts: six points per tooth, depth in mm, plus bleeding, recession, mobility, furcation.
Have the perio probe ready, record exactly as called, and report anything suspicious to the dentist.

summary: You can now convert any tooth to its FDI number, place findings on the correct side of the chart, code surfaces such as MO or DO, recognise common charting abbreviations and symbols, and record a six-point periodontal chart accurately as the dentist calls it.

A.q: The dentist calls 'three-six'. Which tooth is this?
A.why: Quadrant 3 is lower left, and tooth 6 is the first molar.

whyNot.0: The upper left first molar is 26.
whyNot.1: The lower right first molar is 46.
whyNot.3: The lower left third molar is 38.

A.q: While you record a pocket chart, the dentist calls bleeding on probing at one site. What should you do?
options: Note bleeding generally for the whole mouth
Record it at that exact site as stated
Wait until the end and add it from memory
Leave it out unless bleeding is heavy
A.why: Bleeding on probing is recorded at the precise site where it is called, so inflammation can be tracked tooth by tooth.

whyNot.0: A general note loses the site detail the dentist needs.
whyNot.2: Recording from memory risks errors; chart it as it's called.
whyNot.3: Any bleeding on probing is significant; it is the key sign of inflammation.

A.q: While charting, you notice a white patch on the side of the patient's tongue that the dentist hasn't mentioned. What is the correct action?
options: Ignore it, as diagnosis is not your role
Tell the patient it looks like cancer
Record it and inform the dentist
Book a referral to the hospital yourself
A.why: You don't diagnose, but you must record and report anything suspicious so the dentist can assess it.

whyNot.0: Ignoring a possible problem puts the patient at risk; you should report it.
whyNot.1: Suggesting a diagnosis is outside your scope and would alarm the patient.

B.q: What is the FDI number for the upper right second premolar?
B.why: Quadrant 1 is upper right, and the second premolar is tooth 5, so it is 15.

whyNot.1: 25 is the upper left second premolar.
whyNot.2: 14 is the upper right first premolar.
whyNot.3: 45 is the lower right second premolar.

B.q: A patient attends for a full gum assessment. What should you have ready before periodontal charting begins?
options: A rubber dam punch and clamp
B.why: Pocket depths are measured with a graduated periodontal probe, so it must be on the tray before charting starts.

whyNot.1: A Briault probe detects caries between teeth; it isn't graduated for pockets.
whyNot.2: An amalgam carrier is for placing fillings.
whyNot.3: A rubber dam punch is for isolation, not gum assessment.

B.q: Which finding on a six-point pocket chart most strongly shows active gum inflammation?
B.why: Bleeding on probing is the key clinical sign of active inflammation.

whyNot.0: Recession shows past attachment loss, not necessarily active inflammation.
whyNot.2: A 2 mm sulcus without bleeding is healthy.
whyNot.3: A missing tooth is a dental chart finding, not a sign of inflammation.

C.q: The dentist calls 'MO caries' on a lower molar. Which surfaces are involved?
C.why: M is mesial (towards the midline) and O is occlusal (the biting surface).

whyNot.1: Buccal would be B, giving MB.
whyNot.2: Distal and occlusal would be DO.
whyNot.3: Lingual would be L, giving ML.

C.q: Using FDI notation, how is the deciduous lower right second molar written?
C.why: Deciduous quadrant 8 is lower right, and the second molar is tooth 5, so it is 85.

whyNot.0: 75 is the deciduous lower left second molar.
whyNot.1: 55 is the deciduous upper right second molar.
whyNot.2: 46 is the permanent lower right first molar.

C.q: On a standard dental chart, where are the patient's right-side teeth drawn?
options: On the right of the chart
On the left of the chart
C.why: Charts are drawn as if you are facing the patient, so their right side appears on the left of the chart.

whyNot.0: That would be the view from behind the patient, which charts don't use.
whyNot.2: The top row is the upper arch, both sides.
whyNot.3: The orientation is a fixed convention so that everyone reads charts the same way.

reteach.title: Think of a postcode
reteach.question: A postcode narrows down from area to street. How does an FDI number narrow down from quadrant to tooth to surface?

blocks.body: The first FDI digit is the area: which quarter of the mouth. The second digit is the house number along the street, counting back from the midline. The surface letters are which door: mesial (front door, towards the midline), distal (back door), occlusal (the roof). So '36 MO' means lower left quarter, sixth house back, front door and roof. If you deliver to the wrong address, the tooth gets the wrong treatment, which is why accuracy matters so much.

blocks.h: Quadrant numbers (as you face the patient)
blocks.caption: The numbers run clockwise from the upper right, as you face the patient.

blocks.text: Upper teeth have a PALATAL surface; lower teeth a LINGUAL one. Front teeth have a LABIAL surface and an INCISAL edge; back teeth a BUCCAL surface and an OCCLUSAL surface.

explain.body: First digit = quadrant (1 UR, 2 UL, 3 LL, 4 LR; deciduous 5 to 8). Second digit = tooth from the midline (1 to 8 permanent, 1 to 5 deciduous).

explain.caption: Deciduous chart: 54 is the upper right first molar; 85 the lower right second molar.

test.q: Which quadrant does the number 2 represent in the FDI system for permanent teeth?
test.why: Quadrant 2 is upper left; the order runs clockwise from upper right (1) as you face the patient.

explain.body: Some practices and older records use Palmer. Each tooth is numbered 1 to 8 from the midline, and an L-shaped bracket shows the quadrant: the lines point towards the midline and the bite. So the upper right first molar is written 6┘. Deciduous teeth are lettered A to E.

explain.caption: Palmer view: the same teeth as 16 and 36 in FDI, numbered 6 within their quadrant.

test.q: In Palmer notation, how are deciduous teeth identified within each quadrant?
test.why: Palmer labels deciduous teeth A (central incisor) to E (second molar) in each quadrant.

whyNot.0: Numbers are used for permanent teeth in Palmer.
whyNot.2: Quadrants 5 to 8 are FDI deciduous quadrants, not Palmer.
whyNot.3: M and D are surface abbreviations, not tooth letters.

explain.body: Six sites per tooth: mesiobuccal, buccal, distobuccal, and the same three on the lingual or palatal side. Record the depth in mm at each, plus bleeding, recession, mobility and furcation, exactly where they are called.

test.q: Why is the full pocket chart repeated at review after gum treatment?
options: To compare how the tissues have responded
To check the patient's FDI numbers
To decide which crowns to place
test.why: Comparing charts over time shows whether pockets and bleeding have reduced after treatment.

whyNot.1: Tooth numbers don't change between visits.
whyNot.2: Charts don't expire; they are compared.
whyNot.3: Crown planning isn't the purpose of a pocket chart.
